topic.subject: science
topic.title: Reproduction in plants
topic.scope: vegetative propagation, budding, spores, pollination, fertilisation, fruits and seeds, seed dispersal

misconceptions.why: Students primarily observe seed-based growth in their daily lives and gardens.
misconceptions.fix: Many plants can grow new individuals from vegetative parts like stems, roots, and leaves without seeds.

probe.question: Can a potato grow into a new plant without a seed?
probe.wrong_answer: No, all plants must start from a seed.

misconceptions.statement: Budding is a type of growth, not reproduction.
misconceptions.why: The term 'bud' is often associated with flower buds or leaf buds in common language.
misconceptions.fix: In organisms like yeast, a bud is a new individual that eventually detaches to live independently.

probe.question: Is the bud on a yeast cell a baby yeast or just a part of the parent?
probe.wrong_answer: It is just a part of the parent plant growing bigger.

misconceptions.statement: Pollination is the same thing as fertilisation.
misconceptions.why: Both terms are often introduced together and involve the movement of pollen.
misconceptions.fix: Pollination is the transfer of pollen to the stigma, while fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes.

probe.question: If pollen lands on a stigma, has the plant been fertilised?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, pollination and fertilisation happen at the same time.

misconceptions.statement: Insects eat pollen because they are hungry for the plant's food.
misconceptions.why: Students observe insects visiting flowers and assume it is for feeding on the plant tissue.
misconceptions.fix: Insects visit flowers primarily to collect nectar, and pollen transfer is an accidental byproduct of this visit.

probe.question: Why do bees visit flowers?
probe.wrong_answer: They visit to eat the pollen and destroy it.

misconceptions.statement: Seeds are inside fruits only to protect them from being eaten.
misconceptions.why: Students often view 'protection' as the primary purpose of any container or covering.
misconceptions.fix: Fruits serve to protect the developing seeds and also aid in their dispersal to new locations.

probe.question: Why do plants produce fleshy fruits around their seeds?
probe.wrong_answer: To keep the seeds safe from animals so they don't get eaten.

misconceptions.statement: Seeds can only grow if they fall directly under the parent plant.
misconceptions.why: Students observe seedlings growing under trees and assume that is the intended location.
misconceptions.fix: Seeds are dispersed by wind, water, and animals to prevent overcrowding and competition for resources.

probe.question: Why do seeds have wings or hooks?
probe.wrong_answer: They are just decorations; they are meant to fall right under the parent.
